templates.name: Present or describe to an already familiar audience
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Specify or identify a single fact

items.subtype: Present the findings (two findings, numbers misattached in distractors)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Billions of kilograms of spent coffee grounds are discarded each year, most of them in landfills.
• A team of engineers investigated whether the grounds could substitute for a portion of the sand in concrete.
• In initial tests, untreated grounds leached organic compounds that weakened the concrete.
• The engineers therefore charred the grounds by heating them to 350°C in the absence of oxygen, a process called pyrolysis.
• Concrete in which charred grounds replaced 15% of the sand was approximately 30% stronger than conventional concrete.
items.stem: The student wants to summarize the team’s findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The engineers found that substituting charred coffee grounds for 30% of the sand in concrete made the concrete approximately 15% stronger than conventional concrete.
The engineers found that both untreated and charred coffee grounds strengthened concrete, although the charred grounds increased its strength considerably more.
To determine whether spent coffee grounds could replace some of the sand in concrete, the engineers charred the grounds at 350°C.
The engineers found that spent coffee grounds weakened concrete when added untreated but made it considerably stronger once charred through pyrolysis.
items.explanation: The goal is to summarize what the team found. The notes give two findings: “In initial tests, untreated grounds leached organic compounds that weakened the concrete,” and concrete with charred grounds “was approximately 30% stronger than conventional concrete.” Choice D states both findings and the contrast between them, without misusing any figure.

A.why_wrong: It reports a finding, but it reverses the numbers: the charred grounds replaced 15% of the sand, and the concrete was approximately 30% stronger, not the other way around. It also leaves out the finding about untreated grounds.

B.why_wrong: It summarizes two findings, but the notes say untreated grounds “weakened the concrete,” so it is not true that both kinds of grounds strengthened it.

C.recipe: OG (aim and method instead of findings)
C.why_wrong: It gives what the team set out to learn and how it treated the grounds, but it reports neither finding.

items.notes: Subject: technology (spent coffee grounds charred by pyrolysis as a partial sand replacement in concrete). No team, place or date named (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis: no fact-checking); the figures follow the widely reported 2023 result (about 350°C, 15% of the sand, about 30% stronger, untreated grounds leach organics and weaken concrete) and are approximate. Band 7 moves: findings goal with two findings and two numbers; the key drops the numbers and states the contrast; two goal-shaped FALSE options (A swaps the 15% and 30%, B turns the untreated result around) and one OG slot swap (aim plus method), as in 5645f119. No Finding: labels, to avoid cloning the model frame.

band7.why: Findings goal with two findings and two numbers as in 5645f119; the key drops the numbers and states the contrast; A swaps the 15% and 30% and B reverses the untreated result, both goal-shaped; C is the aim and method slot.

items.subtype: Generalization one level up (uses of a system across fields)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1905, American painter and teacher Albert H. Munsell published a system for describing colors.
• He intended it to help art students discuss color with precision.
• The system specifies a color by three properties: hue (such as red or yellow), value (lightness), and chroma (intensity).
• Soil scientists determine a sample’s color by matching it to the printed chips of a Munsell soil color chart.
• Archaeologists use the same charts to document the colors of excavated sediment layers and pottery fragments.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about the uses of the Munsell color system. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Archaeologists use Munsell soil color charts to document the colors of excavated sediment layers and pottery fragments.
Although Munsell designed it with art students in mind, his color system has come to be used in fields well beyond art.
In 1905, American painter and teacher Albert H. Munsell published a color system that specifies each color by its hue, value, and chroma.
Outside of art, the Munsell color system has been used only by soil scientists, who match samples to the printed chips of Munsell soil color charts.
items.explanation: The goal is a generalization about how the Munsell system is used. The notes say Munsell “intended it to help art students discuss color with precision,” yet “Soil scientists determine a sample’s color by matching it to the printed chips of a Munsell soil color chart” and “Archaeologists use the same charts.” Choice B climbs from these two cases to a general claim: a system made for art students is now used in fields well beyond art.

A.recipe: OG (one true specific use, not a generalization)
A.why_wrong: It accurately describes how one group, archaeologists, uses the charts, but it does not generalize about the system’s uses.

C.recipe: OG (true specific about the system’s origin and design)
C.why_wrong: It accurately says when the system was published and how it specifies colors, but it says nothing about how the system has been used.

D.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped generalization with a scope error)
D.why_wrong: It does generalize about the system’s uses outside art, but the notes say archaeologists also “use the same charts,” so it is not true that only soil scientists use it.

items.notes: Subject: science and arts (the Munsell color system, devised by painter and art teacher Albert H. Munsell in the early 1900s for teaching color; its hue, value and chroma; Munsell soil color charts used by soil scientists and archaeologists; well known, no search needed). Band 7 moves: the generalization climbs a level (from two fields to fields beyond art, as in 3b02e88a); two goal-shaped FALSE generalizations (C says other fields reject it, D swaps who it was made for) and one true specific (A). Review: the old C (scientists find it imprecise) and D (made for soil scientists) each died on one bullet; now A and C are true specifics (the 3b02e88a and 2c61e0b9 pattern) and D is a goal-shaped generalization that fails only on the archaeologists bullet; key reworded away from the notes’ “intended it to help art students discuss color.”

band7.why: The generalization climbs a level (two fields to fields well beyond art), as in 3b02e88a; two wrong options are true specifics, and the third does the goal’s job and fails only on one bullet (only soil scientists). Key paraphrases the notes.

fixes: replaced C (scientists find it imprecise, killed by one obvious fact) with a true specific about the 1905 system
rewrote D from a swapped-origin option to a goal-shaped scope error (only soil scientists)
paraphrased the key away from the notes’ wording

items.subtype: Present findings to an audience familiar with the term
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Bortle scale, published by amateur astronomer John Bortle in 2001, classifies night-sky darkness.
• It ranges from class 1, an excellent dark-sky site, to class 9, an inner-city sky.
• A sky quality meter is a handheld instrument that measures the brightness of the night sky.
• In a recent study, researchers compared volunteers’ Bortle ratings of 120 locations with meter readings taken at those locations.
• The volunteers consistently judged the skies as darker than the meters indicated, particularly at suburban locations.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s findings to an audience already familiar with the Bortle scale. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Volunteers rating 120 locations on the Bortle scale consistently judged skies as darker than sky quality meters indicated, particularly at suburban locations, researchers found.
Volunteers in the study consistently rated skies as darker on the Bortle scale, which ranges from class 1 (an excellent dark-sky site) to class 9 (an inner-city sky), than the meters indicated.
The Bortle scale, a nine-class classification of night-sky darkness published by John Bortle in 2001, was used by volunteers who rated 120 locations in a recent study.
Researchers compared volunteers’ Bortle ratings of 120 locations with readings from sky quality meters, handheld instruments that measure the brightness of the night sky.
items.explanation: The goal is to present the study’s findings to readers who already know the Bortle scale. Choice A uses the term without explaining it and gives the finding: the volunteers “consistently judged the skies as darker than the meters indicated, particularly at suburban locations.”

B.why_wrong: It reports the finding, but it spends its middle explaining the Bortle scale’s classes, which this audience already knows.

C.recipe: AUD and PART (defines the scale, gives no finding)
C.why_wrong: It defines the Bortle scale for readers who already know it and never says what the study found.

D.why_wrong: It describes what the researchers compared, but it does not present the result of that comparison.

items.notes: Subject: science (astronomy, light pollution). The Bortle scale facts are real (John Bortle, Sky & Telescope, 2001; class 1 excellent dark-sky site to class 9 inner-city sky). The study is unnamed and generic, with invented numbers (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis). Band 6 by plan (no band-7 AUD_FAM official): two AUD options (B is otherwise complete and fails only by redefining the scale, the cleanest audience test, as in 2.1 D) and one PART.

band7.why: AUD_FAM has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/rhetorical_synthesis.md section 1), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 with an audience-clause trap (B) that also states the finding.

items.subtype: Describe a process (ordered steps, agents swapped in distractors)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Czochralski process, developed by Polish chemist Jan Czochralski in 1916, is used to grow the large single crystals of silicon required for computer chips.
• First, fragments of highly purified silicon are melted in a quartz crucible.
• A small seed crystal attached to a rod is then lowered until it barely touches the molten silicon.
• As the rod is gradually rotated and withdrawn upward, silicon solidifies onto the seed, replicating its crystalline structure.
• The resulting cylindrical ingot is subsequently sliced into thin wafers.
items.stem: The student wants to describe how the Czochralski process forms a silicon crystal. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In the Czochralski process, a seed crystal is lowered into a quartz crucible and melted, and the molten silicon surrounding it is then drawn upward into a cylindrical ingot.
In the Czochralski process, molten silicon is poured over a gradually rotating seed crystal, which replicates the silicon’s crystalline structure as the two cool into an ingot.
In the Czochralski process, a seed crystal touching molten silicon is slowly turned and pulled upward, and silicon hardening onto it copies the seed’s crystalline structure.
In the Czochralski process, a rod withdraws a seed crystal from molten silicon, after which the seed itself is sliced into thin wafers that replicate its crystalline structure.
items.explanation: The goal is to describe how the process forms a crystal. The notes say a seed crystal is lowered “until it barely touches the molten silicon,” and “As the rod is gradually rotated and withdrawn upward, silicon solidifies onto the seed, replicating its crystalline structure.” Choice C gives these steps in order and with the right roles: the seed is turned and pulled up, and the silicon that hardens onto it copies the seed’s structure.

A.why_wrong: It describes a process, but the seed crystal is not melted; only the purified silicon is melted, and the seed barely touches it.

B.why_wrong: It reverses which material copies which: the silicon replicates the seed’s crystal structure, not the other way around, and nothing in the notes says the silicon is poured.

D.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: wrong object sliced, growth step dropped)
D.why_wrong: It skips the step in which silicon solidifies onto the seed and says the seed itself is sliced into wafers; the notes say the ingot that grows on the seed is sliced.

items.notes: Subject: technology (the Czochralski process: Jan Czochralski, 1916; polysilicon melted in a quartz crucible, seed crystal on a rod dipped, rotated and pulled, ingot sliced into wafers; textbook-level facts, no search needed). Band 7 moves: an ordered process in unlabelled bullets (no Step labels, unlike b07a7634); all three distractors are goal-shaped FALSE, each swapping an agent or a step (seed melted, silicon copies seed reversed, seed sliced), as in b07a7634.

band7.why: Ordered process as in b07a7634; all three wrong options describe the process with true parts and fail on one swapped step or agent (seed melted, silicon poured and the copy direction reversed, seed sliced); the key is now paraphrased rather than echoing the bullet.

fixes: key reworded (turned, pulled upward, hardening, copies) so it no longer echoes the fourth bullet word for word; explanation updated

items.subtype: Contrast two items on the named attribute
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In assessing the danger posed by potentially hazardous asteroids and comets, astronomers rely on two scales.
• The Torino scale assigns each object a whole number from 0 to 10.
• It was designed to communicate impact risks to the general public.
• The Palermo scale assigns each object a value that can be positive or negative.
• It was designed for specialists, who use it to compare an object’s impact probability with the background risk.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast the audiences for which the two scales were designed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both the Torino scale and the Palermo scale rate the danger posed by potentially hazardous asteroids and comets.
While the Torino scale was designed to communicate impact risks to the general public, the Palermo scale was designed for specialists.
Designed for specialists, the Palermo scale compares an object’s impact probability with the background risk.
Objects on the Torino scale receive whole numbers from 0 to 10, whereas objects on the Palermo scale receive values that can be positive or negative.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast the audiences the two scales were made for. The notes say the Torino scale “was designed to communicate impact risks to the general public” and the Palermo scale “was designed for specialists.” Choice B sets these two audiences side by side with “While.”

A.recipe: REL (a similarity instead of a difference)
A.why_wrong: It states what the two scales have in common, not how their intended audiences differ.

C.why_wrong: It gives the Palermo scale’s audience but says nothing about the Torino scale, so no contrast is made.

D.recipe: REL (a difference on the wrong attribute)
D.why_wrong: It contrasts the kinds of numbers the scales use, not the audiences they were designed for.

items.notes: Subject: science (astronomy, impact hazard: the Torino scale, whole numbers 0 to 10, for public communication; the Palermo Technical Impact Hazard Scale, continuous and possibly negative, for specialists, relative to the background risk; well known, no search needed). Notes carry two differing attributes so the wrong-dimension option (D) is a real trap; the goal names the audience.

items.subtype: Contrast two items on the named attribute
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Arches enable builders to span doorways and other openings in masonry walls.
• In a corbel arch, each horizontal course of stones projects slightly farther over the opening than the course beneath it, until the two sides converge.
• Corbel arches appear in ancient structures in Greece, India, and Cambodia.
• A true arch consists of voussoirs, wedge-shaped stones arranged along a curve.
• A central stone at the summit, the keystone, locks the voussoirs in position.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in how the two kinds of arches are constructed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Corbel arches, which appear in ancient structures in Greece, India, and Cambodia, enable builders to span openings in masonry walls.
A true arch consists of voussoirs, wedge-shaped stones arranged along a curve and locked in position by a central keystone.
Although corbel arches and true arches both enable builders to span openings in masonry walls, the two kinds of arches are constructed quite differently.
Whereas a corbel arch is built from stone courses that each project farther than the one beneath, a true arch uses voussoirs locked by a keystone.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast how the two arches are built. The notes say that in a corbel arch “each horizontal course of stones projects slightly farther over the opening than the course beneath it,” while “A true arch consists of voussoirs, wedge-shaped stones arranged along a curve,” which the keystone “locks” in position. Choice D joins the two methods with “Whereas.”

A.why_wrong: It tells where corbel arches are found and what arches do, but it never describes how either kind is built.

B.why_wrong: It explains how a true arch is constructed but says nothing about the corbel arch, so there is no contrast.

C.recipe: VAGUE (says they differ without saying how)
C.why_wrong: It claims the arches are “constructed quite differently” but never says how either one is built.

items.notes: Subject: arts (architecture: corbel arch built from projecting courses vs true arch of voussoirs and a keystone; corbelling in Mycenaean Greece, Indian temples and Khmer Cambodia; general knowledge, no search needed). Maya left out on purpose, since item 07 is a Maya subject.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In tracking time, the ancient Maya used several interlocking calendars.
• The Tzolk’in was a 260-day calendar that paired the numbers 1 through 13 with twenty day names.
• It was used primarily to schedule religious ceremonies.
• The Haab’ was a 365-day calendar made up of eighteen months of twenty days and a period of five additional days.
• Together, the two calendars formed a cycle that repeated every 52 years.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the Tzolk’in and the Haab’. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Tzolk’in was a 260-day calendar, whereas the Haab’ lasted 365 days, including a period of five additional days.
Used together, the Tzolk’in and the Haab’ formed a cycle that repeated every 52 years.
The Tzolk’in, which paired the numbers 1 through 13 with twenty day names, was used primarily to schedule religious ceremonies.
The ancient Maya used several interlocking calendars to track time, including the Tzolk’in and the Haab’.
items.explanation: The goal is to point out a difference between the two calendars. The notes say the Tzolk’in “was a 260-day calendar” and the Haab’ “was a 365-day calendar.” Choice A contrasts these lengths with “whereas.”

B.why_wrong: It describes the cycle the two calendars formed jointly, which links them rather than distinguishing them.

C.why_wrong: It describes only the Tzolk’in, so nothing is contrasted with the Haab’.

D.why_wrong: It names both calendars as part of the Maya system but gives no way in which they differ.

items.notes: Subject: history (Maya calendars: the 260-day Tzolk’in of 13 numbers and 20 day names, the 365-day Haab’ of 18 twenty-day months plus 5 days, the 52-year Calendar Round; general knowledge, no search needed). Only one contrast is offered among the options, so the generic goal has a single answer.

items.subtype: Describe to an audience unfamiliar with the object
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Willamette meteorite, an iron-nickel mass weighing approximately 15.5 tons, is the largest meteorite found in North America.
• Discovered in Oregon in 1902, it has been exhibited at New York’s American Museum of Natural History since 1906.
• The Clackamas people of Oregon’s Willamette Valley call it Tomanowos.
• Under a 2000 agreement with the museum, members of the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde hold a private ceremony with Tomanowos annually.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the annual ceremony to an audience unfamiliar with the Willamette meteorite. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Under a 2000 agreement, members of the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde hold a private ceremony with Tomanowos annually.
Discovered in Oregon in 1902, the Willamette meteorite, an iron-nickel mass weighing approximately 15.5 tons, is the largest meteorite found in North America.
Each year, members of the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde hold a private ceremony with Tomanowos, the largest meteorite found in North America.
The Clackamas people of Oregon’s Willamette Valley call the meteorite exhibited in New York Tomanowos.
items.explanation: The goal is to describe the ceremony for readers who do not know the meteorite. Choice C describes the ceremony, a “private ceremony with Tomanowos” held every year, and identifies Tomanowos as “the largest meteorite found in North America,” so an unfamiliar reader knows what the ceremony involves.

A.why_wrong: It describes the ceremony but never says what Tomanowos is, so a reader unfamiliar with the meteorite would not know what the ceremony centers on.

B.why_wrong: It identifies the meteorite clearly but says nothing about the annual ceremony.

D.why_wrong: It gives the meteorite’s Clackamas name and location but does not describe the ceremony.

items.notes: Subject: history and culture (the Willamette meteorite, about 15.5 tons of iron and nickel, found in Oregon in 1902, at the AMNH since 1906; Tomanowos to the Clackamas; the 2000 agreement giving the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde an annual private ceremony; well known, no search needed). The goal names the meteorite as the unfamiliar thing, so the key must identify it, as 2.34 identifies Maloof.

items.subtype: Describe a work to an audience unfamiliar with the artist
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Meschac Gaba is a contemporary artist from Benin.
• Between 1997 and 2002, he created Museum of Contemporary African Art, an installation that takes the form of a museum.
• The installation consists of twelve rooms, among them a library, a game room, and a museum shop.
• One room documents Gaba’s own wedding, which was staged as part of the work in 2000.
• In 2013, London’s Tate Modern exhibited all twelve rooms together.
items.stem: The student wants to describe Museum of Contemporary African Art to an audience unfamiliar with Meschac Gaba. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Museum of Contemporary African Art consists of twelve rooms, among them a library, a game room, and a museum shop.
Beninese artist Meschac Gaba’s Museum of Contemporary African Art takes the form of a museum, with twelve rooms that include a library and a game room.
Meschac Gaba, a contemporary artist from Benin, staged his own wedding in 2000 as part of one of his installations.
In 2013, all twelve rooms of Gaba’s Museum of Contemporary African Art were exhibited together at London’s Tate Modern.
items.explanation: The goal is to describe the work for readers who do not know Gaba. Choice B identifies him as a “contemporary artist from Benin” and describes the work as “an installation that takes the form of a museum” with “twelve rooms,” such as “a library” and “a game room.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the rooms but never says who made the work, which an audience unfamiliar with Gaba needs.

C.recipe: OG (a fact about the artist, not the work)
C.why_wrong: It introduces Gaba but tells only of his wedding, not what Museum of Contemporary African Art is like.

D.why_wrong: It tells where and when the rooms were shown, not what the work is, and it uses Gaba’s name without saying who he is.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Meschac Gaba, Beninese artist; Museum of Contemporary African Art, 1997 to 2002, twelve rooms including the Library, Game Room, Museum Shop and the Marriage Room from his 2000 wedding; shown complete at Tate Modern in 2013; well known, no search needed).

items.subtype: Explain the origin of a name
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the 1940s, Elizabeth Lee Hazen and Rachel Fuller Brown were scientists at the New York State Department of Health.
• Hazen worked in New York City and Brown in Albany, so they exchanged samples by mail.
• In 1950, they announced the discovery of a substance, produced by a soil microbe, that killed fungi.
• It became the first widely used antifungal antibiotic.
• They named it nystatin in honor of the New York State Department of Health.
items.stem: The student wants to explain the origin of the name nystatin. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Hazen and Brown named their antifungal antibiotic nystatin to honor the New York State Department of Health, where they worked.
Nystatin, the first widely used antifungal antibiotic, was discovered by two scientists at the New York State Department of Health.
Because Hazen worked in New York City and Brown worked in Albany, the two scientists exchanged samples by mail.
In 1950, Hazen and Brown announced that a soil microbe produced nystatin, a substance that killed fungi.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain where the name nystatin came from. The notes say Hazen and Brown “named it nystatin in honor of the New York State Department of Health,” where they worked. Choice A states the name and the reason for it.

B.why_wrong: It names the drug and the department where it was discovered but never says the name was chosen to honor that department.

C.why_wrong: It explains why the scientists mailed samples, which has nothing to do with the drug’s name.

D.why_wrong: It reports the discovery of nystatin but does not explain its name.

items.notes: Subject: science (Elizabeth Lee Hazen and Rachel Fuller Brown, New York State Department of Health, nystatin from Streptomyces noursei, announced 1950, first widely used antifungal antibiotic, named for New York State; well known, no search needed). B is the 1.6 C pattern (both halves, no link).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• For centuries, incense clocks were used throughout China to measure time.
• Because incense burns at a consistent rate, the length consumed indicated how much time had elapsed.
• Some incense clocks also functioned as alarms.
• In these, threads with small metal weights at each end were suspended across the incense.
• When the smoldering incense reached a thread, the thread broke and the weights dropped onto a metal plate with a loud clang.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how some incense clocks functioned as alarms. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Because incense burns at a consistent rate, the length consumed in an incense clock indicated how much time had elapsed.
Some incense clocks had threads with small metal weights at each end suspended across the incense.
Some incense clocks could alert people that a chosen amount of time had passed.
When the incense burned through a weighted thread suspended across it, the weights dropped onto a metal plate with a loud clang.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain how the alarms worked. The notes say “When the smoldering incense reached a thread, the thread broke and the weights dropped onto a metal plate with a loud clang.” Choice D gives this chain of events: the fire reaches the thread, the thread breaks, and the falling weights make the sound.

A.why_wrong: It explains how incense clocks measured time, not how some of them sounded an alarm.

B.why_wrong: It names the weighted threads but never says what happened to them or how they made a sound.

C.recipe: VAGUE (states the alarm without saying how)
C.why_wrong: It says the clocks could alert people but gives no explanation of how they did so.

items.notes: Subject: history and technology (Chinese incense clocks, some with weighted threads that drop onto a metal plate as an alarm; general knowledge, no search needed).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Burning Mountain is a hill near the town of Wingen in New South Wales, Australia.
• Beneath it, a coal seam has been smoldering underground for an estimated 6,000 years.
• Geologists consider it the oldest continuously burning coal fire known.
• The fire front advances approximately one meter per year.
• Today the site is part of a nature reserve with a public walking trail.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how long the coal fire beneath Burning Mountain has been burning. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Burning Mountain, a hill near the town of Wingen in New South Wales, Australia, is now part of a nature reserve with a public walking trail.
The front of the coal fire beneath Burning Mountain advances approximately one meter per year.
Smoldering for an estimated 6,000 years, the coal fire beneath Burning Mountain is considered the oldest continuously burning coal fire known.
Beneath Burning Mountain, a hill in New South Wales, Australia, lies a coal seam that is on fire.
items.explanation: The goal is to stress how long the fire has burned. The notes say the coal seam “has been smoldering underground for an estimated 6,000 years” and that geologists “consider it the oldest continuously burning coal fire known.” Choice C combines the figure with the superlative.

A.why_wrong: It describes the site as a nature reserve with a trail and says nothing about how long the fire has burned.

B.recipe: OG (the fire’s speed, not its age)
B.why_wrong: It gives how fast the fire front moves, not how long the fire has been burning.

D.why_wrong: It says a coal seam is burning but gives no sense of how long it has been burning.

items.notes: Subject: science (geology: Burning Mountain near Wingen, NSW, a coal seam fire estimated at about 6,000 years, thought to be the oldest known coal fire, moving about a metre a year, in a nature reserve with a walking track; well known, no search needed).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In weaving, weft threads pass back and forth through the lengthwise warp threads.
• In supplementary weft weaving, extra weft threads are woven in alongside the base weft to create raised decorative patterns.
• Songket is a fabric made in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brunei.
• In songket, supplementary weft threads of gold or silver form shimmering patterns on silk or cotton.
• Songket was traditionally worn by royalty during ceremonies.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an explanation and an example of supplementary weft weaving. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In supplementary weft weaving, extra weft threads are woven in alongside the base weft to create raised decorative patterns.
Supplementary weft weaving adds extra weft threads to create raised patterns, as in songket, whose gold or silver threads form shimmering designs on silk or cotton.
Songket, a shimmering fabric made in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brunei, was traditionally worn by royalty during ceremonies.
In all weaving, including the weaving of songket, weft threads pass back and forth through the lengthwise warp threads.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: explain supplementary weft weaving and give an example. Choice B explains that the technique adds “extra weft threads” to “create raised decorative patterns” and gives songket as an example, in which “supplementary weft threads of gold or silver form shimmering patterns on silk or cotton.”

A.why_wrong: It explains the technique but gives no example of it.

C.why_wrong: It names songket and how it was worn but does not explain supplementary weft weaving.

D.why_wrong: It explains ordinary weaving, not the supplementary weft technique, so it does not explain the term the goal names.

items.notes: Subject: arts (textiles: supplementary weft weaving; songket of Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei, gold or silver supplementary weft on silk or cotton, a royal and ceremonial cloth; general knowledge, no search needed).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Reusable shopping bags have become common in grocery stores.
• Researchers Uma Karmarkar and Bryan Bollinger wanted to know whether bringing one’s own bags influences shoppers’ other purchases.
• They analyzed purchase records from one California store of a major grocery chain.

items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s results. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Karmarkar and Bollinger found that shoppers who brought their own bags were more likely to purchase both organic foods and indulgent foods.
Karmarkar and Bollinger wanted to know whether bringing one’s own reusable bags to the grocery store influences what else shoppers decide to purchase.
To study shoppers who bring reusable bags, Karmarkar and Bollinger analyzed purchase records from a California grocery store.
Shoppers who brought their own bags to a California grocery store were more likely to purchase organic foods.
items.explanation: The goal is to present what the study found. The notes give two results: shoppers with their own bags “were more likely to purchase organic foods” and “were also more likely to purchase indulgent foods, such as cookies and chips.” Choice A presents both results and credits them to the researchers.

B.why_wrong: It states what the researchers wanted to learn, not what they found.

C.why_wrong: It describes the data the researchers analyzed but reports no result.

D.why_wrong: It gives only the organic-food result and leaves out the finding about indulgent foods.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Karmarkar and Bollinger 2015, Journal of Marketing, BYOB: bringing your own bags raised the likelihood of buying both organic and indulgent foods, scanner data from a single California store of a major chain, a licensing explanation). Real study, named; no figures used, only the published direction of the results (WAVE.md: no invented figures on a real study). Review: core claim confirmed against the abstract (Journal of Marketing 2015, doi 10.1509/jm.13.0228: “scanner panel data from a single California location of a major grocery chain”; bringing one’s own bags “increases purchases of not only environmentally friendly organic foods but also indulgent foods”) and the Harvard Gazette summary (licensing effect).

fixes: notes said loyalty-card data from several California stores; the paper used scanner data from one California store (doi 10.1509/jm.13.0228), so bullet 3 and options C and D now say one store and purchase records
finding (organic and indulgent purchases) and the licensing explanation confirmed: real finding, correctly credited

items.notes: Subject: arts (opus sectile, Roman inlay of marble and glass cut to the shape of each part of a design, as opposed to mosaic tesserae; general art-history knowledge, no search needed). items.notes: Subject: science and technology (the Oxford Electric Bell, Clarendon Laboratory, ringing since 1840 on its original dry piles; the Centennial Light, Livermore-Pleasanton Fire Station 6, carbon-filament bulb burning since 1901; well known, no search needed). While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• His journey from San Francisco to New York City lasted 63 days.
• In 1909, Alice Ramsey became the first woman to complete a transcontinental drive.
• Her journey from New York City to San Francisco lasted 59 days.
• Ramsey did all the driving herself; none of her three passengers drove.
items.stem: The student wants to compare how long Ramsey’s journey lasted with how long Jackson’s lasted. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Jackson’s 1903 journey across the country lasted fewer days than the journey Ramsey made six years later.
Ramsey’s 1909 transcontinental journey lasted four fewer days than Jackson’s 1903 journey.
Jackson drove an automobile across the United States in 1903, six years before Ramsey completed her own transcontinental drive.
Alice Ramsey, who did all the driving herself, became the first woman to complete a transcontinental drive in 1909.
items.explanation: The goal is to compare the lengths of the two journeys. The notes say Jackson’s journey “lasted 63 days” and Ramsey’s “lasted 59 days.” Choice B states the comparison correctly: Ramsey’s journey lasted four fewer days.

A.why_wrong: It reverses the comparison: Jackson’s journey lasted 63 days, more than Ramsey’s 59.

C.why_wrong: It compares when the journeys happened, not how long they lasted.

D.why_wrong: It describes Ramsey’s achievement but makes no comparison of the journeys’ lengths.

items.notes: Subject: history (Horatio Nelson Jackson, first US transcontinental drive, San Francisco to New York, 1903, 63 days; Alice Ramsey, first woman, New York to San Francisco, 1909, 59 days, her three companions did not drive; well known, no search needed). Two measures point opposite ways (Jackson first, Ramsey faster), so C is a real wrong-dimension trap, as in 2.44 D.

items.stem: The student wants to make and support a generalization about where some countries have relocated their capitals. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Some countries have moved their capitals from large cities near a coast or border to more central cities, as Kazakhstan did when it moved its capital from Almaty to Astana.
In 1991, Nigeria moved its capital from Lagos, its largest city, to Abuja, a planned city near the center of the country.
Nigeria moved its capital from Lagos to Abuja in 1991, six years before Kazakhstan moved its capital from Almaty to Astana.
Some countries have chosen to move their capitals to cities that are closer to their centers.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: make a generalization and support it. Choice A makes a general claim drawn from both cases, that some countries have moved capitals from cities near a coast or border to more central ones, and supports it with Kazakhstan’s move from Almaty, which “lies near the country’s southeastern border,” to Astana, “much closer to the country’s center.”

B.why_wrong: It describes Nigeria’s move accurately but makes no general claim about countries’ capitals.

C.why_wrong: It compares when the two moves happened instead of generalizing about where capitals were moved.

D.why_wrong: It makes the general claim but offers no case to support it.

items.notes: Subject: social science (geography: Nigeria moved its capital from Lagos to Abuja in 1991, Abuja chosen for its central location; Kazakhstan moved from Almaty to Akmola, renamed Astana, in 1997; well known, no search needed).
